summary: A $30-50k first-year deal sold directly to price-pressured device makers with no security budget line, by a 25-person team, is a long, expensive enterprise sale with no forcing function. Certification only monetises if carriers or retailers require it, and none is committed. The free-report wedge is good; the pricing unit, the validation test and the channel are weak.

objections.objection: No budget owner before a mandate. The buyer is a VP R&D at a maker with no product-security team, in segments (cameras, routers, smart-home) with thin hardware margins. $25k/yr plus $5k per certification competes with BOM cost cuts and features; the concept itself names 'won't pay without regulation' as its riskiest assumption, so the core revenue line has no forcing function at launch.

Certification revenue is a two-sided chicken-and-egg. A $5k certificate is worth paying for only if large distributors, carriers or retailers ask for it, yet the channel plan lists carrier and chip-vendor partnerships as intentions with no anchor partner, and the concept admits a certificate without a recognised standard has limited weight. Incumbent labs (UL) already hold that buyer trust.

Sales motion versus contract value. Direct enterprise sales to mid-size makers, many of whom outsource firmware to ODMs in Asia, implies multi-month cycles, technical pre-sales and security reviews of firmware upload. An ACV of roughly $30-50k barely covers a field rep plus sales engineer at a few deals each per year; with ~25 staff burning cash, the motion needs either much larger deals or a channel that sells for you.

The validation test measures the wrong thing. '4 of 20 makers buy within 2 weeks' of a free report is unrealistic for a $30k+ purchase that needs budget approval; a failure would be ambiguous and a pass is unlikely. A better test is signed paid pilots or letters of intent tied to a named carrier/retailer requirement over a quarter.

Pricing unit and model are muddled. 'Per product line' is ambiguous when makers ship many SKUs on shared firmware and rebuild often; the runtime on-device protection feature implies a per-unit royalty model that is not priced at all; and the comparables have no prices, so 'cheaper than labs and pentests' is unverified.

Renewal and churn risk: once a maker has fixed the top exposures and certified a model, the reason to keep paying an annual subscription is unclear unless re-certification per firmware release is required. The free report may itself deliver most of the perceived value.

strongest_point: A free automated firmware report is a cheap, concrete, low-friction wedge that shows makers real exposures and creates a natural upsell into remediation and certification.
what_would_change_my_mind: A named carrier, large retailer or chip vendor contractually requiring the certification from its suppliers.
3 or more makers signing paid pilots at or above $25k.
Evidence that makers in a high-margin segment (industrial, medical, automotive) already budget for firmware security, supporting ACVs above $100k.
